title: The Empire 2
subtitle: Buried Sun
author: R.E. Smith
description: The war that began in Rising Sun has changed the balance of power, but victory has not brought peace. As rival rulers fight over a buried city and its ancient technology, the past threatens to reshape every kingdom above it.
fullDescription:
The Buried Sun

Book Two of The Empire

Some ruins are buried because the dead deserve peace. Others are buried because the living are afraid of what they might remember.

The war that began in Rising Sun has changed the balance of power, but victory has not brought peace.

Arslan, Xu, Yuelan, and the people caught between their worlds now face the consequences of rebellion, fractured alliances, and ancient forces awakened beneath the earth. The old order is breaking, and every kingdom is scrambling to decide what comes next.

Then the buried city begins to wake.

Beneath forgotten roads and sealed chambers lies evidence of a civilization older than the empires now fighting above it. Its machines were built for purposes no living ruler fully understands. Its history contradicts sacred stories. Its weapons could alter the balance of power overnight.

And everyone wants control of what has been found.

As soldiers move across unstable borders, rulers bargain over survival, families are divided by loyalty, and old enemies become necessary allies. The deeper the excavation goes, the clearer one truth becomes:

The past was not lost.

It was hidden.

The Buried Sun is the second book in The Empire, a completed nine-book adult epic fantasy series of war, political intrigue, ancient technology, dragons, rebellion, love, loyalty, and the brutal cost of building a new world from the ruins of the old.

For readers who enjoy sprawling political fantasy, buried civilizations, morally complicated characters, military conflict, dangerous archaeology, ancient mysteries, and empires shaped by secrets no one was meant to uncover.

The sun did not die.
It was buried.

title: Serpent City
subtitle: When the City Wakes, the Serpent Rises
author: R.E. Smith
description: Beneath New York, artist Rosa Navarro discovers that something ancient is changing her paintings and knows her name. Drawn into abandoned tunnels and a hidden world of shifting reality, she must decide whether the serpent below the city wants her as prey or as its chosen vessel.
fullDescription:
An Ancient Hunger in the City That Never Sleeps

Beneath New York’s crowded streets, something ancient stirs.

Rosa Navarro has always lived with shadows — in her art, her dreams, and the city’s forgotten corners. But when the faces in her paintings begin to change, twisting into visions she can’t explain, Rosa is drawn into a hidden world beneath the skyline. There, in the abandoned tunnels and derelict stations of the city’s bones, she finds whispers of a serpent older than history… and the chilling truth that it knows her name.

As reality fractures and the line between dream and waking blurs, Rosa and her friends are pulled into a game they don’t understand, stalked by an ageless presence that feeds on memory, desire, and fear.

The deeper they go, the more the city itself changes — murals shift, buildings breathe, and the serpent waits in every reflection. To survive, Rosa must face the thing beneath the streets… and decide whether she is its prey, or its chosen vessel.

Perfect for fans of Neil Gaiman, Leigh Bardugo, and urban legends with teeth, Serpent City is a haunting blend of supernatural horror and gritty urban fantasy that will keep you turning pages deep into the night.

title: The Empire Prequel 5
subtitle: The Iron Exile
author: R.E. Smith
description: An unproven accusation sends an exile into a dangerous search for the truth. When contradictory records and a missing bronze key point north, old secrets threaten to expose the fragile foundations of the world before the Empire.
fullDescription:
The Iron Exile

Book Five of The Empire Prequel

The accusation was never proved. The exile survived it anyway.

A missing bronze key should have been an inventory problem.

Instead, contradictory records point north.

One old transfer sheet mentions Temür bronze. Another does not. A copied note suggests a missing register key may have traveled with repair material decades earlier. No one can prove it.

That is enough to begin a review.

The review becomes an audit.

The audit becomes suspicion.

And suspicion begins moving families.

At first, the language remains careful.

Not expulsion.

Review relocation.

Not confiscation.

Examination.

Not guilt.

Restricted bronze.

Each phrase is defensible.

Together, they become a machine.

As workshops close and households are moved, Iron Hearth fills with smiths, children, widows, tools, wagons, records, and people who never planned to become part of anything larger than survival.

From a distant office, the settlement looks different.

A concentration.

A technical center.

Eventually, a fortress.

On the ground, it is workshops, cooking fires, crowded latrines, cousins, debts, children, and one goat standing on a wall someone has labeled defensive works.

Orun Temür knows the danger of records.

His family has spent generations preserving them.

Now the state uses that very continuity against him.

When an official offers to remove Ayla, Arslan, Saran, and their household from relocation review in exchange for one bronze calibration key, the offer contains no threat.

That makes it worse.

Meanwhile, relocation itself becomes an industry.

Wagons.

Storage.

Certified transport.

Approved inspectors.

Replacement craftsmen.

Nothing requires corruption.

Once displacement has a price, someone can always build a business around moving people.

Then Iron Hearth burns.

Families scatter.

Archives officials expected to seize turn out never to have existed in one place. Household records leave beneath blankets beside onions. Children carry spoons, bent nails, and whatever pieces of home fit inside a wagon.

And when the investigation finally weakens, the damage does not politely reverse itself.

The accusation was not proved.

The dispersal remains.

Now the state must confront a harder question:

What does justice look like after return becomes possible?

Some people want their homes.

Some want compensation.

Some want graves.

Some want workshops but not residence.

Some can return and choose not to.

Because the right to go home means very little if someone else gets to decide that home is still where you belong.

The Iron Exile is Book Five of The Empire Prequel, continuing the six-book story of how investigation becomes policy, policy becomes displacement, and institutions can preserve injustice long after the original accusation collapses.

For readers who enjoy political epic fantasy, family sagas, legal systems, forced relocation, contested evidence, ancient technology, institutional power, dry humor, moral complexity, and stories where the most dangerous sentence may be the one everyone agrees sounds reasonable.

They searched for one missing key.
They found an entire people easier to move.

title: The Cries Beneath the Floorboards
subtitle: The Story of Amelia Dyer
author: R.E. Smith
description: London, 1896. Willowbrook House, a once-respectable orphanage, hides locked doors and whispered horrors beneath its Victorian gentility. As the darkness beneath the floorboards stirs, the children and caretakers face a threat that polite society would rather keep buried.
fullDescription:
The Cries Beneath the Floorboards
By R. E. Smith

Beneath the lace and lullabies of Victorian England, something monstrous stirs…

London, 1896. The fog hangs thick over Willowbrook House, a once-genteel orphanage now cloaked in whispered rumors and locked doors. Infants vanish in the night. Hollow-eyed matrons speak in hushed tones. And under the floorboards—where the boards creak and the air grows cold—the cries of the forgotten echo still.

When young constable Edwin Harrow is called to investigate the mysterious deaths surrounding the home, he uncovers far more than criminal neglect. Beneath the orphanage lies a deeper horror—a secret buried in silence, stitched with deception, and soaked in blood.

This is the tale of Amelia Dyer, a woman cloaked in civility and corsets, whose cradle arms once comforted but now conceal. A tale inspired by the real-life "Ogress of Reading," whose crimes rattled an empire and tested the limits of human evil.

What drives a woman to murder the most innocent among us?
And why do some sins refuse to stay buried?

Told in chilling prose and shadowed with historical authenticity, The Cries Beneath the Floorboards is a gothic psychological horror that peels back the wallpaper of Victorian respectability—and finds a bloodstained nursery underneath.

title: Hodge
subtitle: Where No Man Commands Belief
author: R.E. Smith
description: Cast across the sea, Hodge believes faith should belong to conscience, not be controlled by magistrates, ministers, or powerful men. In the New World, his ideas meet a society unwilling to accept them easily, forcing him to confront the cost of conviction and independence.
fullDescription:
Before a man can build a world he must first be thrown out of the old one.

Hodge travels across the sea. He thinks that faith should be a thing, not controlled by magistrates, ministers or men in power.. The New World does not accept gentle ideas. It challenges them.

From the darkness under a ships deck to the tough settlements in a harsh wilderness Hodge sees sickness, fear, judgment, pride and the quiet cruelty that men do when they think God is on their side. Among settlers who are just trying to survive and leaders who want to control what people believe one question starts to matter more than all the others:

Who has the right to tell another man what to believe?

This story is inspired by the life and ideas of Roger Williams. It is about Hodges journey and the struggle for liberty in early America.

As Hodge stands up against the powers of his time he risks losing his family, safety, reputation and home. What starts as a disagreement becomes an accusation. What starts as a matter of conscience becomes a rebellion. And when those in power finally decide there is no place for him among them Hodge must walk into the wilderness with nothing but his conviction, uncertainty and the strong belief that no man should come between another persons soul and God.

This novel is for readers who enjoy stories, about people, early American history, moral conflict, surviving in the wilderness and ordinary men who are forced to take a stand. It explores what it costs to be free before freedom was a concept.

They thought they had thrown him out.

What they had done was set him free.

title: The Sink
subtitle: YOU DON’T LEAVE THE WOODS CLEAN
author: R.E. Smith
description: Roy and Lisa set out for a straightforward day of kayaking, expecting quiet water, laughter, and an ordinary adventure. But the river offers more than they planned, turning a familiar outing into a test of courage, partnership, and survival.
fullDescription:
A simple day on the river was supposed to be the easy kind of tired.

Roy and Lisa push their kayaks into quiet water with the kind of confidence that comes from years of doing hard things together. The plan is straightforward: a clean run, a few laughs, a little sunshine, and home before it’s fully dark.
Then the current starts making decisions for them.

A wrong turn becomes a trap. Familiar water turns strange. The banks close in. The light goes thin. Little problems stack into big ones—gear, fatigue, cold, distance, time—and the river stops feeling like a place you pass through and starts feeling like something that’s watching you back.

As the day bleeds into night, Roy and Lisa have to do what long-time partners do best: communicate when they’re scared, stay sharp when they’re exhausted, and keep moving when standing still feels safer. Every choice has a cost. Every delay narrows the options. And what began as a bad kayak trip becomes a fight to make it out with their bodies—and their bond—still intact.

The Sink: You Don’t Leave the Woods Clean is a tense wilderness thriller about endurance, marriage under pressure, and the quiet terror of realizing the river doesn’t care how prepared you thought you were.

title: Crown of Cinders 2
subtitle: The Ash Accords
author: R.E. Smith
description: After Kethria’s throne-city burns, Sable discovers that peace can be more dangerous than war. As rulers trade in bargains and old debts demand payment, the struggle for power moves from open battle into the shadows of the recovering city.
fullDescription:
The ash never settles in Kethria. It just waits.

After the throne-city burned and the first debts were paid in blood, Sable learns a brutal truth: war is loud, but peace is where the real knives come out. Kings don’t rule with crowns—they rule with bargains. And bargains, in Kethria, are written in ash.

With the realm splintering, rival houses circling, and dragons choosing sides for reasons no council dares admit, a new treaty is demanded: the Ash Accords—a set of laws meant to stop the bleeding… and secretly decide who gets to keep the knife.

But someone is forging the marks.

As paranoia thickens and the streets fill with smoke and whispers, Sable is forced into the deadliest role of all: not soldier, not hero, but enforcer of a peace she doesn’t trust. Every signature costs something. Every concession buys another enemy. And in the shadows, Rook Calver moves where oaths can’t reach—hunting the truth behind the Accords, and discovering that the city’s oldest powers never died. They simply learned to wear new faces.

Because Kethria doesn’t owe peace.

It owes blood.

CROWN OF CINDERS: THE ASH ACCORDS is Book Two of the Crown of Cinders series—dark epic fantasy packed with ruthless politics, dragon-fire consequences, and a world where every promise is a weapon.

Perfect for readers who love grimdark intrigue, high-stakes alliances, and characters who win by paying the price.

A purity crusade is sweeping the streets. Priests preach righteousness while patrician houses sharpen knives behind velvet curtains. In the ruin belt—where the city’s broken bones still jut from the earth—something old watches Rome with the patience of stone.
Two boys are born at the center of it: Aurelio and Remo, twins marked by a secret no one in the city is ready to name. Raised in a world that kills children for rumors, they learn early that truth isn’t what’s spoken—it’s what survives.

And deep in the halls of power, ledgers and seals decide who gets to live clean… and who gets to die condemned.
A king sits on a fragile throne.
The Bloodborn are rising.
And Rome is about to learn what it costs to be saved.

title: Blood of Eden
subtitle: Book One of The Lilith Covenant
author: R.E. Smith
description: Children vanish beneath Castle Noctivar, red bells ring at night, and Lilith remains hungry beneath the mountain. Sevrin Veyr has spent his life obeying his house’s blood laws, but his life among mortals draws him toward secrets that could threaten the vampire order.
fullDescription:
Children vanish beneath Castle Noctivar.
Red bells ring in the night.
And in the dark below the mountain, Lilith is still hungry.
Sevrin Veyr has spent his life obeying the blood laws of his house. Under the name Tomas Rill, he walks among mortals as a simple bread runner, stealing infants from their cradles and delivering them beneath six loaves of black bread to the mountain stronghold of Noctivar. He does not ask why. He does not look too closely. In his world, obedience keeps monsters alive.
Then he meets Eliane.
Marked by the castle, armed with white magic, and dangerous enough to kill the men sent to collect her, Eliane should have been another offering. Instead, she becomes the first person to make Sevrin question the kingdom he serves, the blood he carries, and the lullaby every vampire child is taught to fear.
Together with an ancient priest who knows far more than any holy man should, Sevrin and Eliane descend into the red dark beneath Noctivar, where children sleep under poppy blood, vampires worship Baal, and Lilith waits in her bath of stolen life.
Beautiful. Merciless. Older than Eden.
To break her power, Sevrin must face the truth of his father’s sin, the horror of his own obedience, and the forbidden bond growing between him and the woman he was never meant to save.
But Lilith does not merely want blood.
She wants a door.
And love may open it.
Blood of Eden is a dark gothic vampire novel blending biblical horror, forbidden romance, ancient myth, blood magic, and the terrifying legend of Lilith. Perfect for readers who enjoy seductive monsters, cursed bloodlines, morally gray heroes, dangerous heroines, and horror that bites deep.

author: R.E. Smith
description: Anna Maria is born into a world where servants are disposable and silence is expected. Inside an old European household, she learns the rules that govern power, class, and survival, while the name Von Stockhausen reveals a price far greater than its noble sound suggests.

**VON STOCKHAUSEN** is a name that sounds noble—until you learn what it cost to wear it.

Anna Maria is born into a world that treats servants as disposable and silence as virtue. In the cold corridors of an old European household, she learns the rules that keep a girl alive: work hard, speak little, and never let anyone see what you want.

But wanting is dangerous.

When a whisper becomes an accusation, the village doesn’t hunt for truth. It hunts for certainty. Faith turns sharp. Neighbors turn watchful. And the same hands that once accepted her labor begin reaching for rope, fire, and a clean story they can tell themselves afterward.

**Von Stockhausen: Anna Maria’s Story** is a bleak, intimate work of historical horror—where the real terror isn’t a creature in the forest, but what ordinary people become when fear gives them permission.

title: The Empire Prequel 1
subtitle: The White Stag
author: R.E. Smith
description: Before the Empire, a harsh winter leaves too many heirs and too little grain. After Bayan Khagan’s death, rival claimants begin changing storehouse seals and competing for control, setting the rules, ambitions, and conflicts that will shape the world to come.
fullDescription:
The White Stag

Book One of The Empire Prequel

Before there was an empire, there was a winter with too many heirs and not enough grain.

Bayan Khagan is dead.

Before his body is cold, storehouse seals begin changing.

Aruq wants rules. Qadan wants strength. Kür Qara wants limits no claimant can quietly swallow later. Around them, widows, riders, clerks, herders, smiths, and household leaders discover that succession is not merely a question of blood.

It is grain.

Roads.

Hostages.

Pasture.

Winter.

And who gets to decide which necessity becomes law.

As rival claims harden, thousands of displaced people are forced north through dangerous country. Among them is Aysu, carrying a child and trying to keep a refugee column alive while nobles argue over horses and men offer “protection” with recruitment hidden inside it.

Then a pale stag appears above White Stag Pass.

Some call it Heaven.

Others call it a deer.

The scouts notice something more useful.

Warm ground.

The route beneath the animal may be opening because of something buried in the mountain, something older than the rulers fighting over the world above it.

Survival turns coincidence into story.

Story becomes ritual.

Ritual begins becoming law.

Years later, an antler that never belonged to an ancient standard is mounted in bronze that was never meant to hold it. Men lower their voices near it. Children inherit a legend built from events that were real, even when the meaning placed around them was not.

And beneath the growing myth, the harder questions remain.

Can a ruler limit his own authority once people begin asking him to use it?

Can emergency power remain temporary?

Can a hostage be called a surety without changing what it is?

Can ancient machinery be made safe without rebuilding the system it once served?

And when a civilization needs a road badly enough, how long before “necessary” becomes permission?

The White Stag is Book One of The Empire Prequel, the six-book series revealing how the political traditions, ancient infrastructure, laws, legends, and institutional habits of The Empire were created generations before Rising Sun.

For readers who enjoy political epic fantasy, succession crises, winter survival, ancient technology, dragons, family conflict, law, mythmaking, dry humor, and characters trying to build systems strong enough to survive themselves.

Every empire begins with a story.
The dangerous part is deciding which version becomes history.

title: The Hollow Kingdom 4
subtitle: Outside Claim
author: R.E. Smith
description: Tressa Vale has measured impossible roads, waking bells, and a throne no living ruler should hold. Now a buried lane opens, snow falls in the wrong season, and a claim from beyond the kingdom challenges the laws that have kept its hidden powers contained.
fullDescription:
**A buried lane opens. Snow falls in the wrong season. And a claim from outside the kingdom begins to speak.**

Tressa Vale has measured impossible roads, waking bells, and a throne no living ruler should hold.

But the Hollow Kingdom is changing.

What began beneath Bellharrow has spread into roads, villages, offices, and old graves the Crown would rather leave sealed. Every place Tressa names becomes harder to ignore. Every witness she protects becomes proof that the old kingdom was built on more than bad law. It was built on silence.

Now the silence is cracking.

In Beggar’s Lane, a buried road opens beneath lime, gravel, and denial, revealing the poor who were packed under the royal road and forgotten. In Applecross, snow falls through blooming orchards, warning of a season cut open by force. And at Harrowmere, a black marker splits like an egg, glowing with cold green light and speaking with the voice of Edric Voss.

The road is lying about distance.

The toll is being paid in blood, memory, and office.

And something outside the known order is learning how to claim its way in.

Garran Holt remains at Tressa’s side, wounded, stubborn, and far too ready to spend himself if it keeps her standing. Their bond is no longer easy to deny, but love in the Hollow Kingdom is not a soft refuge. It is a pressure point. A danger. A promise with teeth.

To hold the line, Tressa must decide which claims deserve entry, which ones deserve refusal, and how much of herself she can give before the road mistakes her for a door.

**The Outside Claim** is Book Four of **The Hollow Kingdom**, a dark romantasy series of haunted roads, ancient bells, buried justice, dangerous magic, sharp banter, slow-burn devotion, and a kingdom that refuses to stay under the Crown’s boot.

title: The Hollow Kingdom 9
subtitle: Season Wound
author: R.E. Smith
description: The year is breaking, dragons are answering, and the Crown Chain waits at the heart of a wound in the seasons. Tressa Vale must follow a road that crosses time itself and confront the forces behind the Hollow Kingdom’s unraveling order.
fullDescription:
**The year is breaking. The dragons are answering. And the Crown Chain waits at the heart of the wound.**

Tressa Vale has followed wrong roads, hidden roads, dead roads, and roads erased from every honest map.

Now she must follow one that crosses the seasons themselves.

The Season Wound has opened across the Hollow Kingdom, splitting the land into spring, summer, autumn, and winter where they do not belong. Fields freeze before harvest. Snow blooms with flowers. Autumn brings records no office wanted found. Summer burns through roads that should have stayed buried. Every season carries a memory, a debt, and a warning.

The kingdom is no longer asking to be witnessed.

It is asking to be held together.

At the center of it all waits the Crown Chain, an ancient binding tied to dragons, law, roads, bells, and every failed attempt to force the Hollow Kingdom into one obedient shape. Some want to wear it. Some want to break it. Some want to use it before anyone else can.

Tressa knows what happens when power calls itself necessity.

author: R.E. Smith
description: The emergency may have ended, but its paperwork and restrictions remain. After the First Chain, permits, protected sites, and technical gatherings become tools of control, as a temporary safety system begins to shape the lives of everyone it was meant to protect.
fullDescription:
The Hostage Prince

Book Four of The Empire Prequel

The emergency ended years ago. The paperwork did not.

After the First Chain, the old dangers are no longer mysterious enough to ignore.

Protected sites have rules.

Repair crews need permits.

Technical gatherings require notice.

Records are kept because someone may need them later.

None of that sounds unreasonable.

That is exactly the problem.

A temporary safety rule becomes a form. The form becomes a copy. The copy becomes a records office. Six months becomes a year, then three. Before long, children know which roads require clay tokens before they understand why the rules exist at all.

Naraa remembers when those rules were written.

Her son Saran grows up inside them.

And a rejected hostage notice bearing his childhood name becomes something the family refuses to throw away.

Because governments remember the parts that worked.

Families have to remember what the government tried first.

Years later, peace between powerful houses depends on another old idea given a cleaner name:

guarantees.

Princes, heirs, and relatives travel between courts as living proof that treaties will be honored. Everyone insists they are not hostages.

Everyone also understands what happens if the agreement fails.

The system is meant to prevent war.

Then one of those guarantees dies in custody.

Suddenly every safeguard matters.

Who chose the physician?

Who controlled the road?

Who witnessed the treatment?

Who pays when a person leaves captivity alive but cannot afford to get home?

And what happens to the servant, groom, cook, or attendant when all the laws were written to protect the prince?

At the same time, Orun Temür begins tracing changes in wells and springs near the old Wall systems.

The evidence is real.

The cause is not yet known.

He has inherited a world where one badly worded observation can become rumor, policy, suspicion, or accusation before the original record reaches the next city.

His father gives him simple advice:

Facts do not love you back. That is why they are useful.

The deeper Orun looks, the more uncomfortable the problem becomes. One settlement’s water may depend on a decision that harms another. Complete knowledge could save lives.

Complete knowledge in one set of hands could also recreate exactly the kind of power earlier generations tried to prevent.

The Hostage Prince is Book Four of The Empire Prequel, continuing the six-book story of how temporary safeguards become permanent institutions, how peace creates its own forms of coercion, and how good rules can become more dangerous precisely because they work.

For readers who enjoy political epic fantasy, court intrigue, family legacies, legal systems, ancient technology, contested evidence, diplomacy, hostage politics, dry humor, and characters discovering that civilization is often built one reasonable exception at a time.

Nobody wakes up and decides an emergency has become civilization.
They simply copy yesterday’s answer onto tomorrow’s page.

Tressa Vale knows roads.
As a Crown Works surveyor, she has measured the kingdom’s boundaries in rain, frost, mud, and miserable company. Roads may sink, flood, crack, or take offense at being trusted, but they do not add seven miles to themselves overnight.
The road to Bellharrow has done exactly that.

Old roads are opening. Old claims are answering. A claimant with a polished smile wants what should stay buried. And somewhere beneath Crownmark waits an empty throne tied to bells, blood, law, and the kind of power that turns ambition into ruin.
Tressa was sent to measure a road.
Now she must decide which kingdom gets to live.

THE OLD MAN'S FIDDLE
The Life and Stories of Owen Dixon
A boy lost in the winter woods. An old man the world had nearly forgotten. And a fiddle that would carry his memory for generations.
Thirteen-year-old Edward never intended to find Owen Dixon.
But deep in the winter woods of Rhode Island, a wrong turn leads him to a remote cabin and an old man whose life seems almost too remarkable to be true.
Owen has been a wanderer, trapper, jailbird, circus man, storyteller, and fiddler. He has known hardship, trouble, laughter, and the restless America of the nineteenth century. To most people, he is simply an eccentric old man living out his remaining years beyond the edge of town.
To Edward, he becomes something more.
A grandfather.
A teacher.
A keeper of stories.
As the unlikely bond between the old man and the boy grows, Owen begins passing down the pieces of a life that might otherwise disappear. And eventually, he entrusts Edward with something more enduring than any story:
his fiddle.
Inspired by the documented life of Owen Dixon (1824–1906) and generations of family history, The Old Man’s Fiddle weaves historical record, family tradition, and imagined moments into an intimate story about memory, inheritance, and the quiet ways ordinary people survive the passage of time.
Because perhaps a man really does die twice: once when his life ends, and again when no one remembers his name.
More than a century later, Owen Dixon is remembered.
And somewhere, the music is still playing.

The Valley: Bjorn and the Norsemen is not a tale told by firelight. It’s a march. A hunger. A storm with teeth.

Bjorn’s people have crossed leagues of hard country chasing safety, land, and the kind of future that doesn’t come with Roman chains. But the world doesn’t hand out peace. It tests it. And when the mountains open into a valley that feels too quiet—too certain—Bjorn learns the oldest truth of war:

Some places don’t want you there.

The valley is beautiful in the way a blade is beautiful. It watches. It waits. It takes measurements. Every step forward costs more than the last—food, strength, blood, faith. Men who have survived sea raids and winter crossings begin to crack under something they can’t name. The storm that rolls down from the heights isn’t just weather. It’s a judgment.

And Rome is never far.

As danger tightens, Bjorn must hold his people together with more than steel. He must make choices that stain. He must decide what kind of leader he is when courage stops being a speech and becomes a debt paid in the dark. The Norse don’t pray for mercy. They build their own. But the valley has its own laws—and it collects.

Gritty, brutal, and fiercely human, The Valley: Bjorn and the Norsemen is a historical saga of survival, loyalty, and the cost of pushing into lands that do not forgive.

If you love hard-edged historical fiction, war bands, Roman shadows, and stories where the wilderness is as dangerous as any army… step into the valley.

Just don’t expect it to let you leave clean.

Kethria was built to outlast kings.

It won’t.

Kethria is the Crownlands’ jewel: iron foundries roaring night and day, river trade fat with coin, stone walls that have laughed at siege engines for generations. Inside those walls, power moves the way smoke does—quiet, constant, everywhere. Lords bargain in candlelit chambers. Guilds count favors like they’re prayers. Soldiers hold the line for rulers who don’t know their names. Common folk keep their heads down and their families fed.

In the inferno, choices get simple in the worst way:

  • Hold the gate and die honest.

  • Run the alleys and live hunted.

  • Stand with the Crown and become the villain someone needs.

  • Turn on it and discover you’re not the only one with a knife.

This is a book about the first scream of a long war—the one history always edits into a cleaner sentence. It’s about oaths snapping under pressure, about the cost of command, about the ugly math of survival when monsters aren’t myths anymore and the city’s own heart starts beating against it.

Expect:
Dark, grounded epic fantasy with war-level intensity
Political intrigue where every alliance has a hidden blade
Siege fire and street violence that feels close enough to smell
Hard choices where “right” and “alive” stop being the same thing
A world that rewards ruthlessness, strategy, and nerve

If you like your fantasy with Game of Thrones–style stakes, battlefield urgency, and characters who earn every inch they keep breathing, KETHRIA IN FLAMES will grab you by the throat and drag you through the smoke.

Because Kethria doesn’t fall all at once.

It falls person by person—one betrayal, one broken oath, one burning tower at a time.

Begin the prequel saga to Crown of Cinders.
CROWNS OF BLOOD: KETHRIA IN FLAMES

description: The old Empire is dead, but its laws endure. Beneath the Black Sand Sea, an awakened city offers food, water, protection, and order through ancient systems that still judge bloodlines, debts, and social roles, forcing the living to confront a past that never truly disappeared.
fullDescription:
Black Dawn

Book Three of The Empire

The old empire is dead. Its laws are not.

Beneath the Black Sand Sea, a buried city has awakened.

Its roads still function. Its gates still judge. Its archives remember bloodlines, debts, offices, armies, slaves, rulers, and crimes committed centuries before the living were born. It offers food, water, protection, and order.

It also believes every person belongs somewhere.

And to someone.

Roxana Vardan enters the city hoping to recover missing workers and prevent her father from claiming its ancient power. Instead, she discovers a civilization capable of turning contracts into chains and freedom into an administrative error. Mara and the trapped laborers begin fighting the system from inside, forcing it to confront something its builders never truly understood: consent.

Across the continent, the consequences spread.

Shirin challenges the Vardan empire her father built from debt and inheritance. Lan Su discovers that the River Kingdom has buried the wrong king. Xu finds himself offered something every emperor dreams of: the power to impose justice everywhere at once. Arslan is offered control over the ancient forges, gates, weapons, and dragons.

Every offer comes with the same poison hidden beneath it.

Obedience first. Freedom later.

The buried system does not merely want rulers.

It wants agreement.

It counts movement as consent. Death as participation. Blood as authority. Hunger as leverage. It can rebuild roads overnight, feed starving children, restore lost cities, and command armies without ever believing itself cruel.

As ancient beacons ignite and forgotten armies begin to rise, enemies who once fought one another must somehow build an alliance without creating another empire in the process.

No single ruler can command it.

No single army can save it.

And when the black sun rises over Red Gate, the choice becomes brutally simple:

Accept perfect order...

or defend the dangerous right to choose wrong.

Black Dawn is Book Three of The Empire, a completed nine-book adult epic fantasy series of war, political intrigue, ancient technology, dragons, rebellion, love, loyalty, slavery, freedom, and the terrible price of power exercised for someone else’s own good.

The dawn is black because the sun has returned.
And this time, it remembers everyone.

description: Three months after Arslan’s assassination, the north faces a crisis no sword can solve. fullDescription:
Blood Charter

Book Six of The Empire

They forbade inheritance. Then the armies asked who would sign the next order.

Arslan is dead.

The laws he helped build are still alive.

Three months after his assassination, the north faces a crisis no sword can solve. Qulan commands the strongest lawful military force, but she has no automatic civil mandate. Tura refuses to inherit authority through love. Khasar carries Arslan’s name, grief, and enormous symbolic weight, but no crown, office, or command.

That was the point.

Now everyone has to live with it.

Road councils need contracts signed. Soldiers need lawful orders. Widows need payments. Camps demand representation. Merchants need guarantees that will survive the next election. Armed institutions cannot simply stop functioning while frightened people debate legitimacy.

And frightened people have begun asking whether blood might be easier.

Across the north, factions gather around competing answers. Some want fixed civilian authority. Others want rotating councils, stronger military continuity, or a ceremonial role for Khasar that they insist carries no real power. Every proposal claims to preserve freedom.

Every proposal creates someone who can sign.

Then Xu is badly injured.

For the first time, the Office of Maritime Provision must function without the young emperor who helped build and restrain it. Mei Ren is offered the simplest solution: rule through household, marriage, and motherhood.

She refuses.

The Office continues anyway.

That may be more dangerous than failure.

As rival orders move soldiers before truth can catch them, custody becomes politics, roads become borders, river gates become weapons, and delegates attempting to write a new charter discover that every clause eventually reaches a body.

Who may close a road?

Who can raise troops?

Who controls a child surrounded by armed adults claiming to protect him?

Who governs when the person everyone trusted is dead, wounded, or absent?

And what good is a constitution if nobody obeys it when they are afraid?

The struggle culminates at Kite Ford, where a civilian congress must survive siege, bloodshed, and three days of pressure without surrendering itself to military government.

Blood Charter is Book Six of The Empire, completing the second trilogy of the nine-book adult epic fantasy saga.

For readers who enjoy political fantasy, constitutional conflict, succession crises, military tension, morally complicated institutions, found family, grief, romance, armed diplomacy, and stories where the most important battle may be over who has the lawful right to give an order.

A charter must survive without one.

author: R.E. Smith
description: Before policing became a profession, ordinary people kept the peace by guarding their streets and answering the call to protect one another. We, The Watchmen traces this tradition from ancient English peace-pledges to modern policing, examining the public’s role in law, duty, and community safety.
fullDescription:
Before police were a profession, keeping the peace belonged to the people.

Long before patrol cars, badges, radios, and blue uniforms, ordinary citizens stood watch over their own streets. They answered the hue and cry. They guarded the gates. They were bound by law and duty to protect one another because there was no one else coming.

We, The Watchmen traces that forgotten history from ancient English peace-pledges and watchmen, through the Bow Street Runners, Robert Peel’s New Police, August Vollmer’s professional reforms, community policing, broken-windows theory, and the fractured public debate that followed George Floyd’s death. Along the way, R. E. Smith examines one hard truth: policing was never meant to belong to the badge alone.

Written by one who has served both the public and the police, this book is not an attack on law enforcement, and it is not a blind defense of it. It is a plainspoken call for both sides to remember the old arrangement: the police are drawn from the public, and the public still carries responsibility for the peace of its own neighborhoods.

At a time when trust is thin, anger is loud, and the line between citizen and officer feels more divided than ever, We, The Watchmen offers a grounded, historical, and deeply personal argument for restoring what should never have been lost.

The badge may carry authority.

But the people carry the power.

fullDescription:
Bronze Rain

Book Two of The Empire Prequel

The wells are failing. The desert is opening. And beneath the sand, something ancient is beginning to work again.

Seyra of Black Reed trusts measurements more than promises.

When her family’s well drops below every known mark, she does what generations before her have done: count the depth, limit the draw, record the change, and keep people alive.

Then the water rises.

Without rain.

Soon, buried stone appears beneath the dunes. Bronze-lined openings breathe cold air. Old roads emerge from the sand. Ancient structures begin revealing systems no living engineer fully understands.

The discovery draws everyone.

Gao engineers want to measure it.

White Stag officials want to control it.

Merchants see opportunity.

Laborers see food.

Black Reed families see outsiders building roads, camps, regulations, and authority on top of water their people have depended on for generations.

Nobody begins with conquest in mind.

That does not mean conquest cannot happen.

As excavation expands, competent administration makes the project stronger. More workers arrive. More grain is distributed. More storage is built. More rules are written. Every new success becomes another reason not to stop.

Seyra keeps asking the question officials dislike most:

What happens when the system works exactly as intended, but the ground beneath it does not?

Local records contradict official maps. Wells recover at different rates. Ancient structures shift. Dragons alter their routes. Pressure builds beneath the basin.

Then the sky begins throwing metal.

Hot bronze falls through rain and ash. Roofs collapse. Floodwater cuts evacuation routes apart. Official signs point people toward roads that no longer exist.

And survival depends on the knowledge that never made it onto the government map.

When the disaster becomes known as Bronze Rain, the fight changes.

Now everyone needs a cause.

A mistake.

A saboteur.

Someone whose name can fit beneath the catastrophe.

But Seyra has dates.

Witnesses.

Water marks.

Her father’s records.

And a chronology that refuses to become the story powerful people need.

Bronze Rain is Book Two of The Empire Prequel, continuing the six-book story of how ancient technology, emergency rule, public works, political authority, and perfectly reasonable decisions begin building the world that will one day become The Empire.

A child’s voice.

The Inner Answer.

fullDescription: In the hills of Kentucky, some bloodlines do not fade. They wait. Sixteen-year-old Elias Fugate has always known he is different. His skin carries the strange blue cast of his family line, a mark that makes neighbors stare and churchgoers look away. In Troublesome Creek, everyone has an explanation, but nobody has the truth. When Elias asks why there are no other blue children his age, the answers turn dangerous. His father dodges the past, his grandfather keeps records that should have been burned, and the elders watch him like something promised has come due. The deeper Elias digs, the more he understands that the blue is not just a color. It is an inheritance. Inspired by the real legend of the Blue People of Kentucky, this is a dark Appalachian gothic novel of family secrets, buried sins, mountain folklore, and one boy’s fight to learn what his bloodline has hidden for generations.

title: The Hollow Kingdom 10
subtitle: Last Treaty
author: R.E. Smith
description: Tressa Vale has survived impossible roads, buried claims, dead roads, and the Crown’s attempts to erase the truth. Now the roads have answered, the dragons have stood, and every old power must face the Last Treaty, the reckoning that will determine what kind of kingdom remains.
fullDescription:
**The roads have answered. The dead have been counted. The dragons have stood. Now every old power must face the Last Treaty.**

Tressa Vale has survived the wrong road to Bellharrow, the waking throne, the First Road, the songless dead, the Outside Claim, the Witness Tree, Sanctuary, the Unrecorded Road, and the Season Wound.

She has measured what should not move, named what the Crown wanted buried, and helped build a First House where witness matters more than power.

Now Barrowgate comes for her.

The old center of Crown Works measure has not forgotten how to command roads, cages, records, bells, children, and bodies. It still believes a wound can be named, seized, transported, and closed. It still believes usefulness is ownership.

It is wrong.

When Barrowgate sends a child turned into a bell mouth, the final war begins without banners. Valehurst must scatter records, hide children, protect witnesses, and hold long enough for the deeper road to open. Beneath the old bridge, Tressa, Holt, Mara, Branoc, and the others enter Hollow Edge, where Crown roads cannot command and the last treaty begins to take shape.

But no treaty can survive if it repeats the old crime.

The Crown cannot rule below. The Hollow cannot own the living. The dragons cannot remain weather engines. The dead cannot become offices. Children cannot be proof. Bodies cannot be payment. Measure cannot become ownership. And Tressa Vale cannot be turned into the map that saves everyone else.

With Holt’s fire nearly spent and every ally carrying wounds of their own, Tressa must face Lock Seven, Barrowgate’s hidden records, the Empty Crown Record, and the final question waiting beneath every road in the Hollow Kingdom:

Can a kingdom be saved without giving it a ruler to devour?

**The Last Treaty** is the final book in **The Hollow Kingdom**, a dark romantasy series of dangerous roads, ancient bells, buried law, fierce witness, dragon-bound seasons, found family, gothic mystery, sharp-tongued allies, and a love strong enough to refuse every throne that asks for blood.

title: The Hollow Kingdom 7
subtitle: Counted Dead
author: R.E. Smith
description: The First House has survived its first night, but danger remains. At Northwatch, Tressa Vale helps create a place where the dead can be counted and the living can refuse to be used, until a bitten apple, a haunted well, and a bloodless white room threaten the fragile hope taking root.
fullDescription:
**A bitten apple. A haunted well. A white room where no one is allowed to bleed.**

The First House has survived its first night.

That does not mean it is safe.

Tressa Vale has helped build a place where the dead can be counted and the living can refuse use. At Northwatch, witnesses gather under snow, law, hunger, grief, and the stubborn hope that truth can become more than a wound.

Then a bitten apple appears on the eastern road.

Inside it waits a map.

The trail leads to the Well Road, where Bessa Dinn’s voice rises from the dark and points them toward Sanctuary. A name that should mean safety becomes something far worse: white gloves, polished halls, quiet bells, and mercy sharpened into control. In Sanctuary, pain is hidden, grief is cleaned, and children are altered until the living can look away more comfortably.

Bessa is still alive.

But not whole.

Garran Holt’s fire, Mara’s body-law, Branoc’s transport cunning, and Tressa’s chain are pushed into a rescue where every hallway has learned to sound gentle while doing harm. Getting Bessa out is only the first fight.

Because Sanctuary has patrons.

They come to Northwatch with dogs, armed retainers, sealed claims, and a white-wrapped wagon that screams before anyone inside it can speak. The child within is called Little Grief, and his name, body, voice, and pain have all been divided for other people’s comfort.

Now the First House must hold a hearing under siege.

No forced return. No sealed claim. No patient as property. No grief made clean for the living.

But the small door is still waiting.

Before third dawn, the Hollow Kingdom demands one who chooses, one who paid, and an answer full enough to pour.

**The Counted Dead** is Book Seven of **The Hollow Kingdom**, a dark romantasy series of haunted roads, ancient bells, gothic mystery, dangerous mercy, fierce found family, slow-burn devotion, and a kingdom where even the dead are finally given standing.

subtitle: Witness Tree
author: R.E. Smith
description: Tressa Vale has followed impossible roads through buried bells, stolen memories, false claims, and Crown offices that turned people into useful things. Now the road leads north toward Northwatch, where the dead gather and the first true witness house may be born in blood.
fullDescription:
**The dead are gathering. The road is counting. And the first true witness house may be born in blood.**

Tressa Vale has followed impossible roads through buried bells, false claims, stolen memories, and Crown offices that turned people into useful things.

Now the road leads north.

Northwatch waits beyond the Green Mile, the King’s Cup, and Kingless Ford, each place returning another piece of what the kingdom tried to take. Edric Voss is being restored one stolen fragment at a time. Oran’s old wound is opening into something no royal court can safely name. Children, ghosts, claimants, and broken witnesses are beginning to gather around Tressa’s chain.

The Crown wants order.

The Gentleman wants payment.

The Hollow Kingdom wants answer.

At the Outer Mark, beneath first snow, Tressa and Holt must help found what should have existed long ago: a First House where claims are heard one at a time, bodies are not vessels, and the dead are not converted into convenient silence.

But witness is dangerous.

Every name entered creates standing. Every truth spoken threatens old power. And when Crown Relief arrives from the storm wearing silver closed-eye masks and carrying bell-metal spears, the First House will have to prove it can stand before it has even finished being written.

Garran Holt’s fire can hold back some monsters. Tressa’s chain can answer some claims. Neither can make the cost gentle.

Because the Witness Tree has taken root.

And once it begins to write, no crown, creditor, office, or kingless road can pretend the dead were never there.

**The Witness Tree** is Book Five of **The Hollow Kingdom**, a dark romantasy series of haunted roads, ancient bells, dangerous law, sharp-tongued allies, slow-burn devotion, gothic mystery, and a kingdom where even grief demands standing.

title: The Empire Prequel 3
subtitle: The First Chain
author: R.E. Smith
description: After the disaster at First House, the ancient network beneath the roads can no longer be dismissed as a buried curiosity. Stations respond to heat, pressure, vibration, and unknown signals, and the effort to prevent another catastrophe begins creating the first chain of control.
fullDescription:
The First Chain

Book Three of The Empire Prequel

They survived Bronze Rain. Now everyone wants to make sure it can never happen again.

That is how the first chain begins.

After the disaster at First House, the ancient network beneath the roads can no longer be dismissed as buried curiosity. Stations respond to heat, pressure, vibration, and signals nobody fully understands. Roads once thought ordinary begin revealing older purposes.

At Western Lamp, water runs uphill.

A bronze throat hums beneath the ground.

A child notices patterns the instruments miss.

And every new answer creates three more questions.

The governments of White Stag and Gao begin connecting what Bronze Rain exposed. Engineers test buried stations. Officials classify routes. Maps are standardized. Access is restricted. Local knowledge becomes strategic information.

The work is careful.

Measured.

Often responsible.

Which makes it even harder to see where caution ends and control begins.

Because the old roads do not belong only to governments.

They cross farms, wells, caravan routes, pastures, and communities whose families knew the land long before officials began calling it infrastructure. A goat path can become strategic overnight simply because a map says so.

Then there is Ash Neck.

The dragon is not attacking cities. She is following something.

Warm seams.

Old vents.

Buried lines.

Whenever crews activate the ancient network, her routes change with it.

Selen wants to understand why.

Tuvan wants to make sure she cannot reach a working station.

Both have evidence.

Neither has certainty.

The argument becomes brutally simple:

Move the road.

Or move the dragon.

When another required test draws Ash Neck into a staffed corridor, the state chooses capture.

Not because she is declared evil.

Not because anyone proves she is hostile.

Because she has become unpredictable in a place the government has decided must function.

The operation succeeds.

Men die.

Horses die.

Ash Neck survives in chains.

And once she is inside the walls, captivity immediately begins acquiring procedures, titles, ledgers, handlers, medical rules, custody agreements, and permanent records.

By the third morning, someone has already written the word permanent.

The First Chain is Book Three of The Empire Prequel, continuing the six-book story of how ancient infrastructure, public safety, political necessity, and fear slowly become institutions powerful enough to outlive the emergencies that created them.

For readers who enjoy political epic fantasy, dragons treated as living creatures rather than symbols, ancient technology, engineering, law, contested land, institutional power, family, dry humor, and moral choices where every side has enough truth to be dangerous.

A chain does not become permanent when the lock closes.
It becomes permanent when everyone learns to live around it.

In Crown of Cinders: The City Owes Blood, power doesn’t march in daylight—it signs its name and lets the bells do the killing.

Sable Rook has survived long enough to know one rule: in this city, innocence is just debt you haven’t been forced to pay yet. When the Synod begins tightening its grip—turning law into scripture and scripture into a noose—Rook is pulled into a struggle where names matter more than swords, and a single ledger can topple districts like rotten beams.

But something older is waking beneath the stone. A voice that shouldn’t exist rides the seams of doors. A crown doesn’t simply sit on a head—it chooses, it hungers, and it opens what was meant to stay shut. As allies fracture, enemies smile from behind clean titles, and the city’s “order” starts to smell like ash, Rook must decide what to save and what to burn… even if the fire takes her with it.

This is adult epic fantasy—grim, fast, and razor-edged—where politics and blood run in the same channels, magic has rules that bite, and every victory comes stamped with a cost.

Because the city owes blood.
And sooner or later, it collects.

author: R.E. Smith
description: Nine months after Blood Charter, the north has become more stable and attractive to people fleeing oppressive governments. But as refugees arrive and strange changes unsettle the land, leaders must decide how to protect their borders without allowing protection to become another form of tyranny.
fullDescription:
Border Fire

Book Seven of The Empire

They built a country people wanted to enter. Then the border asked what protection was allowed to become.

Nine months after Blood Charter, the north is more stable, more lawful, and more attractive to people fleeing governments that are neither.

Then the refugees begin arriving.

At Daran Well, warm water rises where cold water should be. Animals refuse old roads. Bronze hums beneath human hands. Smoke spreads across the southern horizon, and villages empty north before anyone understands whether they are running from civil war, something beneath the earth, or both.

At the frontier, Qulan faces the problem every successful state eventually creates:

People want in.

Families arrive hungry, wounded, armed, frightened, and carrying laws, debts, loyalties, grudges, and claims from the country behind them. The Charter can give water without citizenship. It can give medical care without allegiance. It can protect a camp without annexing the land beneath it.

The harder question is what happens when violence follows the refugees to the line.

Ashar March does not ask to be conquered.

It asks for help.

That distinction becomes the center of the war.

As local councils petition for association, the Charter must decide the difference between asylum, residence, representation, military protection, and membership. Qulan is eventually invited across the old frontier under a narrow defense mandate, only to discover how quickly temporary protection becomes checkpoints, searches, food control, road closures, armed patrols, and foreign troops who are still there tomorrow.

Xu and Mei Ren confront the same problem from the coast as relief ships and armed escorts risk becoming something larger. Ilyara fights to write limits strong enough to survive fear. Samira Veyran, a former Saffron tax clerk, enters Charter protection with her children and discovers that a functioning system can be both humane and unsettling. Rakhim Saren must decide whether loyalty to his country requires obedience to men destroying it.

And beneath every political argument, something older is changing.

Water heats without cause. Bronze vibrates. Compasses fail. Dragons alter their routes. Old roads behave strangely.

The evidence is real.

The explanation is not.

By the time war reaches Kestrel Gate, Mazar Quay, and Three Arches, the question is no longer whether the Charter can win.

It is whether it can help another country survive without quietly becoming its ruler.

Border Fire is Book Seven of The Empire, opening the final trilogy of the completed nine-book adult epic fantasy saga.

For readers who enjoy political fantasy, refugee crises, military intervention, border conflict, constitutional tension, morally complicated warfare, dragons, found family, romance, occupation pressure, and fantasy where doing the right thing does not automatically give anyone the right to rule.

A border can keep an army out.
It cannot keep history buried.

fullDescription:
Rising Sun

Book One of The Empire

Two suns rise. Only one can own the dawn.

Red Gate was supposed to be a summit.

Instead, it becomes the opening move in a conspiracy involving Jade forces, the White Stag, the Temür, and crimes inherited from a generation that believed the past could remain buried.

Arslan returns to the fortress and finds Yuclan waiting there, along with old loyalties, old wounds, and a political trap built from the sins of their parents. When Shen Ru attempts to expose the operation, he is destroyed. Temür settlements come under attack. Survivors scatter. And Arslan’s private losses become the spark of a rebellion he never intended to lead.

At the Jade court, Emperor Xu discovers that his own authority has been used without his consent. He can still choose the throne.

Or Yuclan.

He chooses.

The decision fractures the balance of power.

A dragon is freed. Red Gate breaks. Arslan escapes north with survivors and an army, while Xu watches the same dawn from the opposite side of the Wall.

What begins as a conspiracy becomes a living war.

Rising Sun launches The Empire, a completed nine-book adult epic fantasy saga of rebellion, loyalty, political power, ancient forces, inherited guilt, war, love, and the terrible cost of deciding what kind of world should rise from the ruins of the old one.

For readers who enjoy sprawling political fantasy, morally complicated characters, ancient mysteries, warfare with consequences, shifting alliances, and empires built as much by choices as by swords.

Every empire begins with a decision.
This one begins at dawn.

Now it must survive what comes after.
Something is changing beneath the city—down in the buried veins of old Rome, where stone remembers names that were never meant to be spoken again. The new regime holds the gates and the councils, but the streets are restless, the rooftops are tense, and the ruin belt is louder than ever.
Aurelio carries the weight of a founder—he must keep Rome from tearing itself apart.
Remo carries a mark that won’t cool, a hunger that won’t stay quiet, and a rage that won’t be ruled.

That becomes legend—or a grave.
In the final volume of Wolves of Tiber, the external threat is defeated… and the internal fracture hardens into something permanent.
Because in Rome, power doesn’t just demand sacrifice.
It chooses who will make it.

Beneath an ancient sanctuary in Bronze Age Mesopotamia, Lilith and Baal have built the first blood covenant. But Lilith’s covenant is older than mercy, Baal cannot be buried like a man, and victory may only teach the darkness how to survive.

Children of the First Blood is Book Zero of The Lilith Covenant and the ancient origin story behind Blood of Eden. Brutal, mythic, and blood-soaked, it tells how the first vampire covenant was broken, how the first warning was written, and how one forbidden son learned that blood can open doors, but choice decides what walks through them.

title: The Empire 9
subtitle: The Final Road
author: R.E. Smith
description: Across Tartaria, ancient barriers rise, roads obey dead authority marks, and water systems fail as buried mechanisms begin enforcing rules no living government understands. The roads are closing by memory, forcing a final choice between saving the system and saving the people who depend on it.
fullDescription:
The Final Road

Book Nine of The Empire

They can save the system. They can save the people. They cannot guarantee both.

The roads are closing.

Not by decree.

By memory.

Across Tartaria, ancient barriers rise from buried stone. Roads sort wagons according to dead authority marks. Water systems fail. Mountains fracture. Dragons abandon old ranges. Long-buried mechanisms begin enforcing classifications no living government recognizes and no living ruler authorized.

The Deep Meridian is failing.

And for the first time, everyone knows enough to understand what that means.

The same buried network capable of regulating water, stabilizing roads, controlling pressure, and holding a continent together also carries the machinery of classification and command that earlier empires learned to weaponize. It is not evil. It is not a god. It is not a mind waiting to be defeated.

It is infrastructure.

And it still works.

That makes the choice worse.

As routes collapse and refugee columns begin moving, a new emergency office is proposed: First Command.

One authority.

One chain of communication.

One system capable of coordinating armies, engineers, transport, food, roads, and evacuation across the entire crisis.

It saves time.

It reduces losses.

It works.

And Qulan refuses to take it.

Then Khasar is offered something even more dangerous.

Permanent synchronization.

His unusual compatibility with the Deep Meridian could allow one living person to coordinate the network strongly enough to stabilize much of physical Tartaria. Roads could reopen. Water could move. Pressure failures could be contained.

Cities might survive.

Millions might survive.

All it would require is rebuilding the central point of control the entire series has spent eight books learning to distrust.

And putting a fifteen-year-old boy inside it.

While politicians argue over First Command and engineers fight to understand a system collapsing beneath their feet, the final objective changes.

Not victory.

Evacuation.

Qulan and Ochen hold the northern roads long enough for civilians to move. Xu and Mei Ren turn the Office toward a maritime evacuation involving ports, hospitals, families, food, and hundreds of thousands of displaced people. Lan Su must destroy water systems she spent years learning to save. Huan watches mountains empty and dragons flee. Rakhim opens the southern road into Ashar while fighting men determined to close it.

At Red Gate, the archives are triaged.

Some records are saved.

Some are deliberately destroyed.

And some disagreements are preserved because history without dissent would only become another weapon.

The final war spreads across cavalry roads, harbors, rivers, mountains, and the buried heart of Red Gate.

But there is no throne left to win.

Only time.

Time to move the children.

Time to move the wounded.

Time to move the records.

Time to open one last road before the system that built an empire tears the land apart beneath it.

The last question of The Empire is not who deserves to rule.

title: The Empire 8

author: R.E. Smith
description: When a mountain opens, it reveals not a god or buried king but ancient infrastructure: galleries, bronze mechanisms, water regulators, roads, and sealed interfaces. As the ground itself begins issuing orders, the people above must confront the systems that have quietly shaped their world for generations.
fullDescription:
Ash Meridian

Book Eight of The Empire

They promised to leave when asked. Then the ground began giving orders.

The mountain has opened.

What waits inside is not a god, a prophecy, or a buried king.

It is infrastructure.

Ancient galleries, bronze mechanisms, water regulators, road systems, sealed chambers, and buried interfaces stretch beneath a continent whose people have spent generations fighting over the ruins above them. The deeper investigators go, the harder one truth becomes to ignore:

The old world was not merely built on top of these systems.

It was built around them.

At the same time, the political victory of Border Fire begins creating a quieter danger.

Ashar March asked the Charter for protection. Now Charter soldiers guard roads, Charter engineers keep water moving, Charter ships carry food, Charter courts settle disputes, and Charter institutions have become woven into daily life.

Temporary help is becoming permanent dependence.

And dependence has a way of looking remarkably similar to occupation when everyone involved is competent enough.

Qulan must prove that an army invited onto foreign soil can actually leave it. Xu and Mei Ren confront systems whose usefulness makes withdrawal painful. Ilyara and Neris fight over the difference between consent written into law and consent that remains meaningful after people depend on what they are being asked to surrender.

Khasar, now old enough to understand what people see when they look at him, wants an ordinary life of horses, roads, tools, and work.

The ancient systems have other measurements.

As water failures spread and buried regulators begin responding across distant regions, scholars give the connected network a name:

The Deep Meridian.

It can regulate water.

Open roads.

Stabilize failing systems.

Move food faster.

Perhaps even prevent catastrophe.

But the same machinery once classified people, controlled routes, recognized authority, and decided who was permitted to pass.

When one ancient regulator is deliberately reactivated to save lives, it works.

That is the problem.

Soon old roads begin sorting travelers. Forgotten barriers rise. Supply routes open for some and close for others according to rules no living government wrote. The temptation is no longer theoretical.

Perfect infrastructure has returned.

So has the authority buried inside it.

Meanwhile, Ashar prepares to decide its own future.

Remain permanently inside the Charter.

Or leave.

The Charter has always claimed association is voluntary.

Now it must prove that promise while enemies gather, supply systems strain, and withdrawal makes everyone less safe.

By the time the last checkpoints come down, one border has been removed by human choice.

Another rises from beneath the earth.

Ash Meridian is Book Eight of The Empire, the middle novel of the final trilogy in the completed nine-book adult epic fantasy saga.

For readers who enjoy political fantasy, ancient technology, buried civilizations, military occupation, constitutional conflict, archaeological mystery, dragons, morally complicated institutions, family, romance, and stories where the most dangerous machine is the one that genuinely works.

They learned how to live without an empire.
Now the earth remembers how to build one.

author: R.E. Smith

fullDescription:
**The throne is empty. The roads are waking. And the Crown has not finished measuring the dead.**
Tressa Vale survived the buried throne beneath Crownmark, but survival did not end the danger. It only proved the Hollow Kingdom was real.
Now the floor rings beneath her feet.
The old roads are answering from every direction. Bellharrow. Greyveil. Applecross. Crownmark. Places bound by buried law, broken bells, forgotten claims, and debts the living never paid properly. The Crown wants order. Royal Survey wants control. The Hollow Kingdom wants witness.
Tressa is caught between all three.

He is also becoming harder to keep at a safe distance, which would be inconvenient even if the kingdom were not actively trying to rearrange itself under their boots.
Then Royal Survey reveals the fifth measure.
Obedience.
It is older than law, cleaner than murder, and far more useful to people who prefer their crimes official. In the capital, roads can be made straight, bells can command, and the dead can be filed away until no one has to remember who gave the order.
Tressa, Holt, Mara, and Voss must enter the machinery of Crown power before the first road wakes fully and every claim below the kingdom is forced into one obedient line.
But the Hollow Kingdom was never built for one ruler.
And the first road does not open for cowards, kings, or liars.

author: R.E. Smith
description: Thirteen-year-old Ruadh Rìgh MacSweyn grows up in the painted highlands beyond Rome’s walls, where his father rules by hard law and harsher consequences. As Rome advances through fire, hunger, and betrayal, the young heir must prove he has the nerve and judgment to lead his people.
fullDescription:
Rome doesn’t conquer the north with honor. It conquers it with fire, hunger, and men willing to sell their neighbors.

Ruadh Rìgh MacSweyn is thirteen when the world starts sharpening around him. In the painted highlands beyond the empire’s walls, his father—Angus Mór, chief of the MacSweyn túath—rules by hard law and harder consequence. Ruadh is the heir… if he can prove he has the nerve to lead, the stomach to spill blood, and the spine to survive the kind of betrayal that comes smiling.

Then Ruadh meets **Sìne**—a girl from a neighboring tribe he’s not supposed to touch, let alone love. Their courtship begins in secret at the Highland games and burns into an oath the clans never approved. It also paints a target on them both.

Because rivals are everywhere.

Neighboring chiefs and their sons want the MacSweyn seat and will do anything—poison, lies, hostage-work—to claim it. **Beli of the River Mouth** plays friend while feeding Rome the gaps in the north. And Roman scouts circle the forests like wolves, baffled by warriors who don’t march in lines, who vanish into trees, who strike at night and melt into the land as if the land itself fights back.

As Rome pushes deeper into Caledonian territory, tribal politics turn brutal. Love becomes leverage. Loyalty becomes a blade you either hold… or feel in your ribs. The pressure peaks at **Mons Graupius**, where Ruadh marches into his first true battle and learns the ugliest truth of war:

Sometimes the worst slaughter happens behind the lines.

By the time the smoke clears, Ruadh is eighteen—crowned by loss, hunted by rivals, and forced to lead what’s left of his people into exile. With Dunvegan burning behind them and the western sea ahead, the survivors gamble everything on hired ships and a new home on **Benbecula**.

It isn’t a happy ending. It’s a survived ending.

**RUADH RÌGH: ASH AND OATHS** is a gritty, adult historical epic—part romance, part blood-soaked survival—where the north fights an empire, clans fight each other, and a young Mor learns that a crown isn’t gold…

…it’s ash held together by oaths.

* Political betrayal, tribal warfare, and hard-won leadership

title: The Empire 5
subtitle: Iron Levy
author: R.E. Smith
description: Eight months after Salt Crown, the famine has eased, grain is moving, and roads are open, but the emergency institutions remain. Relief offices and armies have discovered how useful they are, raising a dangerous question: will the systems built for survival ever surrender the power they gained?
fullDescription:
Iron Levy

Book Five of The Empire

The famine taught governments what survival cost. Peace teaches them how many soldiers that cost can buy.

The emergency is ending.

The armies are not.

Eight months after Salt Crown, the grain is moving again, the roads are open, and the worst of the famine has eased. But the institutions created to survive it have discovered something dangerous:

They are useful.

Relief offices now control ships, payrolls, repair yards, armed escorts, debt powers, and contracts. Families that once signed for food now sign for wages. Villages trade service for security. Young men and women discover that a uniform can pay burial debts, buy seed, provide medicine, and keep a household alive.

No one calls it conscription.

Not yet.

Orri knowingly signs a three-year service contract because the money can save his family. He understands that soldiers fight and sailors drown.

What he does not yet understand is how quickly the purpose of an army can change after the signature is dry.

Across the continent, the machinery of defense begins hardening into something permanent. Xu must decide whether emergency military authority can be dismantled without leaving millions exposed. Qulan commands forces created for defense while civilian governments fear the soldiers they now depend upon. Boro fights a system capable of turning deserters into criminals and poverty into recruitment. Arslan watches political disagreements acquire uniforms, ships, weapons, and payrolls.

Every argument now has armed men standing behind it.

Then the violence begins.

Blue Reef.

East Chain.

Iron Yard.

Greywater.

Broken Chain.

Each battle, riot, fire, assassination, and military order makes the next emergency easier to justify. The same societies that learned to price famine are learning to price soldiers.

And when Arslan is murdered at Red Gate, grief does what no law has managed to do.

It mobilizes armies.

Forces that were created to protect free people begin marching toward one another, each carrying lawful orders, legitimate grievances, dead friends, and enough iron to turn a political crisis into continental war.

The final question is no longer whether military service is good or evil.

It is harder than that.

If a person freely agrees to one dangerous purpose, how much can the state change that purpose before consent becomes obedience?

Iron Levy is Book Five of The Empire, the second novel in the series’ second trilogy and part of the completed nine-book adult epic fantasy saga.

For readers who enjoy military fantasy, political intrigue, naval warfare, morally complicated alliances, soldiers caught between duty and conscience, dragons, romance, assassination, mass battles, and fantasy worlds where laws can become weapons long before anyone draws a sword.

The army is already here.
The question is who gets to point it.

author: R.E. Smith
description: After the First House survives its first siege, Tressa Vale continues the work of witness at Northwatch, where every answer reveals another buried room beneath the kingdom’s clean records. fullDescription:
**A hidden road waits beyond the door. No map records it. No Crown office admits it exists.**

The First House has survived its first siege.

That should mean the worst is behind them.

It is not.

At Northwatch, the work of witness continues, and every answer digs up another buried room beneath the kingdom’s clean records. Empty white Sanctuary shoes appear in the snow, each pair requesting review. Winter’s broken crown wakes in seven dangerous shards. A blue bird key points toward a quiet nursery room beneath Greyveil. And old ledgers begin to reveal the shape of a system larger than any one office.

Children were not only taken.

They were traded.

Crown, Hollow, Sanctuary, Voss, Wardenry, Vale, Road, and Outside all left marks on the stolen, the hidden, and the misnamed. Tressa Vale has built a house where truth can stand, but truth is beginning to arrive faster than any ledger can hold it.

Then Crownmark opens another wound.

At the East Archive stair, a woman hidden beneath gray cloth is revealed: Maereth Ysmark, a royal living return classified as dead and used when the Inner Answer child could not answer. Her existence threatens Crown continuity, Queen Ysabet’s rule, and the old machinery that kept inconvenient bloodlines locked away from daylight.

Garran Holt stands beside Tressa through every new breach, every old bell, every map that tries to correct itself around her. Their bond has become stronger than caution and more dangerous than either can name. But love does not make the road safe. It only gives them another reason to keep standing.

Because beyond the small Northwatch door waits something older.

An unrecorded road.

Stakes wrapped in cloth line the dark ground. Some cloth bears names. Some bears teeth marks. Some bears nothing at all. And far between the black trees, something carries a lantern and speaks as if it has waited a very long time.

The First House has learned to read.

Now the road that was never written is ready to answer.

**The Unrecorded Road** is Book Eight of **The Hollow Kingdom**, a dark romantasy series of haunted roads, buried children, ancient bells, fierce witness, gothic mystery, slow-burn devotion, sharp-tongued allies, and a kingdom whose hidden records are finally opening.

In a world rebuilt by flame…

What happens when the fire answers back?

Salt Crown

Book Four of The Empire

The first trilogy broke the chain. Now someone has arrived offering to finance the repair.

Fourteen months after Black Dawn, freedom has survived.

Barely.

Principle does not fill a granary.

And it can save lives.

Its power grows through salt, grain, ships, insurance, debt, wages, harbor access, and contracts freely signed by people who may have no meaningful alternative. The crown in Salt Crown is no piece of gold. It is the name ordinary people begin giving to a system that can rule without ever sitting on a throne.

As famine tightens its grip and a storm fleet pushes every alliance toward breaking, old enemies must cooperate again. But this time the question is not whether they can defeat a tyrant.

The False Peace

Book Six of The Empire Prequel

The wars are over. The roads are open. The markets are full. Peace has finally arrived.

Then Altana finds a goat in an accounting ledger.

A hill family failed to provide two men for a spring road crew. One son was sick. The other was away with sheep. The father was lame.

The district took a goat.

No soldiers beat anyone. No house burned. No one died.

The road was cleared.

Peace remained excellent.

Months later, the goat appears beneath a harmless phrase:

LOCAL BURDEN BALANCING.

Altana begins looking closer.

A charcoal family fined for missing transport duty.

A river settlement charged after refusing storage seizure.

A northern clan penalized for failing to provide escorts.

Different governments.

Different rules.

The same pattern.

Powerful houses negotiate before obligation.

Weak communities discover the terms after refusal.

Peace is reciprocal at the top and compulsory at the bottom.

No council ever wrote a law saying:

Hurt the weak to preserve peace.

No one had to.

One policy avoided burdens likely to provoke retaliation.

Another shifted those burdens elsewhere.

Another favored communities least able to resist.

Each rule made sense alone.

Together, they formed a machine with no single inventor.

But Altana's investigation uncovers something darker than unfair taxation.

Old ledgers point toward private experiments involving ancient material.

Fear.

Blood.

Human subjects.

A note hidden inside a binding claims the mysterious pearl-like substance responds better after fear.

The claim may be wrong.

That does not make it harmless.

Because people believed it enough to hurt others trying to prove it.

The trail moves north.

Records disappear into family property, government offices, merchant networks, and forgotten winter stores. Not every missing page is conspiracy. Sometimes history vanishes because someone gives a ledger to a brother and assumes winter will keep investigators away.

Sometimes that is enough.

Now Altana, Shen, Vahram, Orun, and the people who inherited generations of laws, compromises, and carefully preserved evidence must decide whether peace can be repaired without destroying the institutions holding it together.

Because the system is not failing.

That is the problem.

It is working exactly as generations taught it to work.

The False Peace is Book Six and the conclusion of The Empire Prequel, completing the story of how necessity became procedure, procedure became institution, and institution became the world inherited by Rising Sun.

For readers who enjoy political epic fantasy, buried conspiracies, institutional power, ancient technology, legal intrigue, family legacies, investigative mysteries, dry humor, and stories where the final enemy is not a monster or a king, but a system everyone helped build.

Peace did not become false because the fighting stopped.
It became false when everyone agreed not to count who was paying for it.
